hook: In February 2023, earthquakes struck southern Türkiye and northern Syria. Within days, UN satellite analysts began comparing images from before and after to map damaged buildings across many towns, a job teams on foot could not do as quickly. Maps like these help aid groups decide where to send help first. Data about places are not just facts: they decide where help, money and services go.

figure.caption: Data lead to decisions by people and organizations at different scales.

chain.cause: A government counts its people in a census, or a satellite images the ground
chain.effect: decision makers learn how many people live where and how places are changing

chain.cause: Leaders share money, seats or services by those numbers
chain.effect: the data shape where schools, clinics, pipes and aid go

chain.cause: The data are out of date, miss people or hide differences inside an area
chain.effect: decisions can send resources to the wrong places

ideas: A census is an official count of all the people in a country, often every ten years, with facts about households.
Census data and satellite images inform decisions by individuals (where to buy a house), businesses (where to open a store) and governments (where to build, how to share seats and money).
These decisions happen at every scale: a school board (local), a national agency, a group of countries or the whole world.
Every source has a limitation of data: censuses age and miss people; satellites cannot see through clouds or into homes; data for a whole city hide its neighborhoods.

misconception.wrong: Official data such as a census are complete and always up to date.
misconception.right: A census is taken every few years and misses some people, such as those without a fixed home. Good decisions say how old the data are and who may be missing.

summary: Census data and satellite images are powerful because decisions follow them: where a family buys a home, where a company opens a store, where a city lays pipes, how a country shares seats and money, and where aid goes after a disaster. They inform choices at every scale, from a block to the world. Every source also has limits: censuses age and undercount, satellites miss what clouds or roofs hide, and data for large areas hide what happens inside them.
